nodes.title: Why Communities Keep Dying in the Same Two Ways
nodes.opening: Most communes of my acquaintance traded inner freedom of the heart (spirituality) for outer freedom (secular, nondogmatic, political). The two pendulum ends of this trade-off mirror each other. I believe we can combine the best of both, but first, let’s see how each fails individually.
nodes.ending: To give an example of striking the balance: My contemplative practice is grounded in the early Buddhist suttas , with a critical reading. Most are treasure, while some are obviously late additions (sometimes to the point of real absurdity). A living community should relate to its own teachings in that same critical manner while staying devoted to following what they’ve decided on so far.
nodes.reader_question: Why have the available models disappointed?
nodes.purpose: Show the recurring split between outer freedom and inner healing, then articulate the desired combination.

nodes.title: Outer-freedom-only models
nodes.opening: The secular communes (and all the manuals I’ve seen on building them) had a solution for how to distribute property or labor in a way folks could agree on, but when the deep waters of jealousy or childhood hurt or humiliation or attraction or resentment or grief came up, the group was without a common method for dealing with it.
nodes.ending: Eventually, when people are together long enough, politics will become a way of carrying emotional material that people can’t name. There will be a fight about a schedule or committee or noise or food or some policy or other, but it won’t be about that. There’s no shared way to talk about the hurt itself, but the meeting agenda is the one place the group lets you push for something and win, so the angry communard goes there, trying to get some justice.
nodes.reader_question: What does procedural freedom fail to address?
nodes.purpose: Show emotional material becoming politics when no shared practice can address it.

nodes.title: Spiritual dogma models attempting inner freedom
nodes.opening: Many people have already realized that they are more interested in spiritual (or emotional) liberation than political liberation, so they tend to congregate in communities built for that. But because these communes focus so much on the inner work that the founder believes in, it can often look like some kind of prison-monastery cult, where you feel free inside as long as you don’t question anything.

From what former members have shared, the community’s doctrine ran deep into members’ intimate decisions. This is how it often goes: folks talk about oneness with the universe, while one man defines what the universe is.

nodes.purpose: Expose dependence on a founder’s doctrine while retaining the value of inner practice.

nodes.title: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
nodes.opening: In 2005, a few college buddies (Emile & Dolores) and I went down to Oventik, one of the Zapatista caracoles (”snails”), the regional centers that tie their villages together in Chiapas. We almost died several times getting there. The muddy mountain road ran along cliffs without guardrails, and our rental car was on its last legs, which is a great combination when you’re on your way to visit a revolution.
nodes.ending: Sociocracy has a very different history, yet some similar features have emerged there as well: circles, decision-making by consent, distributed authority, and linking between the levels. Does this prove there’s a universal formula? No. But it means that people building institutions of this sort have another serious system to study, instead of inventing their governance during their first dispute.

nodes.title: Zap spirituality enigma
nodes.opening: I felt a deep spirituality from the Zapatistas. The Mayan language, as they explained, doesn’t even have subject/object structure. Instead of “I put the glass there” it’s something like “With me, the glass moved there.” I also suspect there may be a private relationship they have with ayahuasca, since Mimosa hostilis (a potent DMT ayahuasca plant) mainly comes from that region, and the Mexican government vaguely accuses them of narcotrafficking. That’s another reason to look at them as an example of much of my model, since if they are using ayahuasca, it could explain some things about their political struggles and spiritual successes, including the fact that they have the most beautiful poetic rhetoric I’ve ever seen published.

nodes.title: Democratic anarcho-communalism actualized
nodes.opening: What impressed me the most was how they do authority. It’s mandar obedeciendo , to lead by obeying: the representatives carry the decisions people made in the assemblies, and they have to answer to the people who gave them the mandate.
nodes.ending: The Fire and the Word describes the movement growing from family to village, village to region, and region to larger structures. It also gives one of the most useful Zapatista principles for community design: build the practice first and develop the theory afterward. The autonomous municipalities came first; an association of them became a rehearsal for the Good Government Juntas (Boards). When different municipalities encountered different problems and uneven progress, that experience generated another structure rather than being forced to fit the original plan.

nodes.title: Real democracy is a continual struggle
nodes.opening: After a long internal review, in 2023, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving their previous federated governmental structure, which was split into Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. The original idea was to have power vested in the local communities, but it had crept up and consolidated itself at higher levels over time for practical reasons. Their new arrangement moved authority downward toward a Local Autonomous Government in each community.
nodes.ending: But there is a special reason the Zapatistas were successfully able to reverse this degeneration. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories. They share language and family ties. They’ve fought land struggles together, and defended themselves together for decades.

nodes.title: Exporting Zapatismo via the Escuelita
nodes.opening: For the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita (little school). The goal of the escuelita was to expand their anarcho-communal, spiritual-humanist revolution worldwide. Outsiders came from all over the world, lived with host families there and learned autonomy by taking part in day to day life. Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.
nodes.ending: But despite actually trying to train people in their model, the Zapatistas themselves have been clear that people shouldn’t expect to directly or easily import/export their philosophy ( Zapatismo ) as something ready-made, shake & bake. A new ecovillage can’t copy the diagram everyone can see and get the trust underneath it right away.

nodes.purpose: Explain learning autonomy through everyday participation and the limits of exporting it.

nodes.title: Money is still a problem
nodes.opening: Now, the Zapatistas also don’t prove my whole money-free economy goal. They still use money internally in some cases, not others, and they still use it externally for trade. They’ve also benefitted from outside economic help, while at the same time making efforts to remain politically independent from donors and more self-sustaining.
nodes.ending: One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents spend their lives performing community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities there are. A week of feeling transformed isn’t what it’s for. It’s for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build somewhere else.

nodes.opening: Part of it is integration: an insight needs somewhere to land. What happens when you come back from an amazing experience which gave you insight and clarity about your life, into the same old environment where nobody knows what you’ve been through and you’re faced with the same old cues? It can be super helpful to have gone through the experience in a community, where the people who held you through it can also notice what happens to you over the following months. The deeper you go, the more alienated you can feel. After my original ayahuasca ego deaths at age 25, I had trouble finding anyone in the physical world who seemed to have experienced anything similar. I couldn’t even find them at Buddhist monasteries despite all the preaching about enlightenment. That helped give me a God complex, a Savior complex, or both, which then attracted exactly the right people to show me my limits. 😂 In a community of people who’ve sat through the same nights, you aren’t the only one who’s been there, and someone can catch the God complex early. Do you trust the people you’re relying on for support? Support from people you trust is different from paid support, which is often paying people you don’t know to look after you for a night. Sometimes they’re great, but sometimes the person with the feather has only known you for 4 hours and already has a cosmology to explain everything you say. In a community, your sober sitter may be someone who’s known you for years, and you feel the difference between being watched and being held. This is especially important when doing iboga or other long and medically risky experiences. For those you need to be properly screened beforehand and monitored continuously. Your peers can also reality check any downloads you may have had. Psychedelics can give you insight and they can give you convincing nonsense, all in the same bright shining light. A few friends who know your history may notice the difference between new understanding and… mom. One of the benefits of community is rhythm , and many traditional medicinal practices occur within ceremonies that have a communal schedule. The shared schedule of ceremonies, rather than each person doing ceremonies when they want, can serve to limit compulsive use and provide for integration time. There are the practical benefits: logistics are easier when it comes to things like having childcare arranged by the group that parents are comfortable leaving their kid(s) with, not needing to drive away from the ceremony, having someone bring water to someone or just sit quietly with them while they come back to normal consciousness, etc. And if you scream in release, the neighbors and landlord don’t call 911. And then there will be people to play with! Raves often let strangers fast-track intimacy (getting to a level of intimacy that usually comes after building trust), but imagine doing ecstatic music & dance in a community that already knows each other (and each other’s inconvenient habits). 💃🕺

nodes.title: The Case Against Psychedelics
nodes.opening: Physical and psychological negative effects of ayahuasca were common in the Global Ayahuasca Survey , although severe effects were far less common and context mattered. And these medicines can open things up faster than a person (or their group) can deal with. One of the best resources on this topic is the Challenging Psychedelic Experiences project .
nodes.ending: They do also attract people who are all for revelation and hate the follow-through, people who can collect 12 ceremonies and 6 origin stories and still can’t say sorry to their housemate. Any community based mainly around the peak experience is going to find out sooner or later that the insight doesn’t do the practical work for it. Sometimes the dishes need doing and a scared kid needs comforting.

nodes.title: Legality and Public Practice
nodes.opening: Most of the writing on communities hasn’t caught up with psychedelics. They’ve gone from taboo toward regulated use really fast ( licensed service centers for psilocybin started opening in Oregon in 2023, Colorado set up a system for regulating natural medicines and began licensing in 2025, and New Mexico enacted a Medical Psilocybin Act in 2025), and Australia has allowed authorized psychiatrists limited access for a list of conditions since 2023, for both psilocybin and MDMA.
nodes.ending: Most intentional communities using psychedelics are still not public about it, due to possible trouble (even where the law allows some use) from parents worried about children, from neighbors imagining chaos, from insurance providers who might drop them, and from local officials who may not understand any of the distinctions.

nodes.title: No Special Shamans
nodes.opening: Traditional lineages usually disagree with me on this, and many ayahuasca tribes and Bwiti iboga communities believe the medicine should stay under trained lineage authority. I respect what those traditions have preserved, and I’ve learned some “dos & don’t dos” from their sensible practices and less sensible practices. For example, although I do highly value loving kindness meditation , inner child reparenting , and nibbana meditation before ceremony, during, and at all times, I notice a lot of people want their ceremony to look and feel like some kind of abstract mix of indigenous rituals & props to make it feel more authentic and sacred than their everyday life. I understand the benefit of setting aside one time and place for sacred experiences (the book, “God is Red” comes to mind), although the shadow side to that is making the spiritual seem like another world apart from your regular life, which is sort of opposite to integration.
nodes.ending: Still, I want people to learn to guide themselves and care for each other, within the limits of their competence.

nodes.title: After the Psychedelic Calling
nodes.opening: A lot of people feel the urge to form a village after going through some serious psychedelic and/or mystical experiences. Finding their people and helping others get to whatever just opened up is part of the same urge. That call may be real, but forming a community based on omnipotence is a terrible idea.
nodes.ending: Once the euphoria wears off and people have a more sober view of the call they feel, it can become useful. A community can be a place for people to train up in the practices, and sometimes go off and start another experiment. In fact, if people are training there so they can help others build communities of their own, they’d be working towards forming a real alternative. That answers the reasonable objection that communes are just privileged escape pods, which gets double dipped with the objection that psychedelics are also privileged escape pods (or, alternatively, as some say, “a vacation for the poor”).

nodes.title: Practice Before Committing
nodes.opening: So, build the part of community you actually can. Call it a practice group , for now, not a commune. Fun and nice things first give incentive. Have a weekly meal with two households. Set up a counseling exchange with one friend, in person or by video call. Share tools or childcare. Transport or food prep work too. Or a sauna. And if you’re hippie enough, add acro-yoga, dance improv, a mothers’ circle or a cuddle puddle .
nodes.ending: Until all of those phases are passed thru, you’re all still promising strangers, and you don’t want to take out a mortgage together yet. And once you’re past those phases, if you still want to live together, you can all meet in a rented or borrowed space, or at each other’s houses, long before anyone needs a land surveyor.

nodes.title: The Math of Absorption, and Who This Isn’t For
nodes.opening: Many perfectly intelligent grownups would rather sit around for six hours talking about solar panels than talk about jealousy, God, death, childhood, money, sex, psychedelics, or somebody wanting to leave, which is what I ask people to do in this article.
nodes.ending: You have a need that far outstrips your free resource right now. This doesn’t mean you’re bad or doomed, it’s about timing; it just means you need to take a first step of finding support where you are and building up your resources. If you don’t have a free resource calculator on hand, an easy way to tell is if you’re running from some crisis right now and mainly need a place to land, get treatment, housing, legal aid, etc. A founding group shouldn’t pretend it can give you those. You want the feeling of village life but don’t want to take on governance, maintenance, conflict, care, etc. You’re not willing to look at yourself when jealousy or conflict comes up.

nodes.title: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
nodes.opening: Any community that lasts will eventually be reorganized by attraction and pair-bonding. When two exes live in the same city, they can move to different sides of the city. When they’re part of a thirty-person commune, they may still be in the same barn the next morning, working in the same team, attending the same meetings, sharing childcare and the same friends. A couple’s jealousy or breakup becomes a problem for the entire community, because it will change the loyalties, the sleeping arrangements, the labor, the kids, the alliances, and sometimes who’s leaving.
nodes.ending: There are some ways the group can help, and basic boundaries the group can enforce, without deciding what type of relationships people have. Even so, there will still be disagreements about this. That’s more realistic than saying it’s all been resolved.

nodes.title: Communal Parenting Adds On
nodes.opening: One of the biggest reasons I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff’s The Continuum Concept . It’s one outsider’s interpretation of the Ye’kuana, an Indigenous people of the Venezuelan rainforest she lived with, and she may have idealized what she saw, but it’s still a powerful picture: the babies are carried along in ordinary adult life, the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and it doesn’t fall on one exhausted parent to be a child’s whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.
nodes.ending: Tamera’s Children’s Place has semi-repeated some of this old Kibbutz philosophy, taking children away from biological parents, because their founders’ ideology said that children are traumatized by the nuclear family and its unstable romantic underpinnings. On the other hand, their actual practice did allow parents (including fathers) to sometimes stay with their children in Children’s Place, so they weren’t as dogmatic as I originally thought.

nodes.purpose: Distinguish distributed care from separating children from secure parental bonds.

It’s one outsider’s interpretation of the Ye’kuana, an Indigenous people of the Venezuelan rainforest she lived with, and she may have idealized what she saw, but it’s still a powerful picture: the babies are carried along in ordinary adult life, the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and it doesn’t fall on one exhausted parent to be a child’s whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.
old.ending: Tamera’s Children’s Place has semi-repeated some of this old Kibbutz philosophy, taking children away from biological parents, because their founders’ ideology said that children are traumatized by the nuclear family and its unstable romantic underpinnings. On the other hand, their actual practice did allow parents (including fathers) to sometimes stay with their children in Children’s Place, so they weren’t as dogmatic as I originally thought.

nodes.title: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
nodes.opening: My own bias is still toward a system where kids are not solely taken care of by their parents, while still honoring the parent-child bond. If the father is unknown, the whole community can do the fathering, but the biological mom’s role should always be honored, since that attachment is formed already from years of nursing. Kids do need their own territory, places where they can create their own society, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.
nodes.ending: Sometimes we also need to protect people from the rare, but real threat posed by dangerous children. I looked through the research corpus for a well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to others. I was looking to find the reported conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I couldn’t find one. It’s possible that records are private, or that cases were referred elsewhere. Whatever the reason, I can’t claim communities already know how to handle the hardest cases on their own. In those cases, the child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review, hopefully including non-intrusive help from outside the home community.
nodes.reader_question: How do children get autonomy without losing protection?
nodes.purpose: Keep agency, ordinary adult bonds, reporting and protection usable together.

nodes.title: The Door Must Open Outward at Adulthood
nodes.opening: If a community’s kids never leave, it has no way of knowing whether they’d come back freely. So let them study, travel and make friends, encounter other ways of living, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors. And kids coming back isn’t necessarily the best thing for the communal movement either. If they then start their own communities, we may see more evolution than if they simply return and continue what their parents started.
nodes.ending: Belonging and freedom should go hand in hand.
nodes.reader_question: Will grown children be free and able to choose their next life?
nodes.purpose: Make departure and possible return or new communities meaningful rather than compulsory belonging.

nodes.title: Every childhood narrows the future
nodes.opening: Most ordinary parents aren’t going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, “Go see the world!” They’ll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work, so they can become self-sufficient, and eventually take care of their aging parents. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and basic survival may rightly come first.
nodes.ending: Belonging and freedom should go hand in hand.

nodes.purpose: Balance survival constraints with transferable skills, records, relationships and feasible next steps.

nodes.title: Money, Land, and Shared Resources
nodes.opening: What kind of legal or illegal entity (cooperative, trust, association, company, or tribal squatting?) will hold the land? This needs to be decided before it’s bought or occupied. Then you’ll need to decide who has what voting rights, who has what access and use rights to common resources, how you will account for people’s contributions (if at all), how inheritance works, outside debts… oh my! Read the founderism questions next, and agree on the exit terms in “Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution” before anyone commits.
nodes.ending: None of this does away with scarcity or economic power. There are lots of areas where such power can be wielded: access to food storage, housing, tools, land, medicine, transportation, and the outside world’s currency, to name a few. Even in a moneyless community, someone can control what’s scarce. Who decides how these things are budgeted and distributed? What do members owe one another? What happens when someone wants to leave?
nodes.reader_question: What are we materially committing to?
nodes.purpose: Separate land, rights, resources and money stages from the preliminary practice group.

nodes.title: Founderism: The Four Questions
nodes.opening: In every community there was somebody (or some founding group) who took the initiative to get it started. They found the land, wrote the first documents, taught the method, recruited the first members, or kept things going when everybody else lost interest. Like the U.S. Founding Fathers.

When it’s tricky and dangerous for everyone like that, I think the commune needs to step in and help people decide how to communicate with outsiders.

nodes.purpose: Make formal and informal power inspectable, including the author’s own potential power.

nodes.title: From One Community to a Movement
nodes.opening: The problem of how these communities stay connected does eventually need to be solved somehow, if the idea is for them to spread without building another state. It should be solved in a way that allows help between communities and the movement of people and knowledge, and also keeps the differences alive, so communities can keep learning from one another. At the federation level, that outward purpose gets concrete: spreading healing practices, training people, seeding new projects, and keeping any one comfortable enclave from thinking it’s the whole movement.
nodes.ending: Some experiments (like a different land system, or a different population size, or any number of rules that work together) can’t be tried in a way that’s cheap. They may look bad when they’re starved of the assets they actually need. “We tried it in one room for three months” isn’t always a fair test.

nodes.title: Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution
nodes.opening: Good people leave for good reasons -- dying parent, love, work, health, exhaustion, change of mind, etc. You don’t want them to lose everything they’ve put in. That’s coercive -- they HAVE to stay if they can’t afford to go, and a community of prisoners isn’t ideal. Whether or not you use money, you’ll need to have a way of providing people with resources when they leave (cash, if you use it, but also tools, transportation, temporary housing, stored up goods, the right to keep using something, or whatever). Otherwise their “right” to leave is only on paper -- it only works when the community happens to have spare money. Write up the exit terms while leaving is still only theoretical -- like a pre-nup when you’re planning the wedding. Not romantic, but protective. Much easier than doing it once anybody’s furious.
nodes.ending: Institutions and relationships don’t die at the same time, and some of what people learned to give one another may go on too. What a relief! The film American Commune follows two sisters who grew up on The Farm. When one of them later became ill, former members who hadn’t seen her in years reached out with support. The Farm’s communal economy had changed dramatically, but the bonds hadn’t vanished.
nodes.reader_question: What happens when living together ends?
nodes.purpose: Distinguish voluntary departure, protective removal and institutional dissolution after commitments are visible.

nodes.title: When Somebody Has to Go
nodes.opening: A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. There may be times when someone has to go. If someone is a serious or generalized danger to others, or keeps violating essential boundaries, or for whatever reason just makes everyday life together impossible for everyone else, it can be the right call to eject them. If restorative work can help in a reasonable amount of time, all the better. But it’s not the community’s job to be a treatment program for someone who’s endangering everyone else.
nodes.ending: Also decide on a mediator or ombudsperson in advance. Why bother? People often won’t trust someone they haven’t already met, who comes in during a crisis as a “neutral stranger.” A mediator doesn’t obviate the need for evidence, safeguarding, rulings, etc. Mediation is an attempt to restore good relations between people. When people can’t or won’t consent to being in community any more, they still need a final separation.
nodes.reader_question: How can removal protect people without becoming abuse?
nodes.purpose: Retain cause, fair process, evidence, independent review and support during separation.

nodes.title: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
nodes.opening: I live in Sénégal, where “intentional community” often sounds like a strange Western phrase. People here are like, “Don’t human beings already do that?”
nodes.ending: But these days it can be soul destroying. People have a lot less of the communal life that held the obligation up (the shared land, work, childcare, food and daily belonging), but they still carry it. So if one of them makes it into the cash economy, it’s really hard to build any independence or long-term stability, because they may be expected to carry everybody. How can they get ahead, when all these people are dependent on them? And the relatives stay dependent too, since the payments don’t give them a real alternative. It’s the ancestral ethic playing out inside an individualistic cash economy. It can keep people alive, but it eats away at both sides too.
nodes.reader_question: What changes when communal life is inherited rather than newly assembled?
nodes.purpose: Ground the proposal in present lived surroundings, warmth and serious limits.

nodes.title: All is not well in paradise
nodes.opening: Does this mean I think Sénégal is some magical place that’s kept its communal paradise? No, not quite. The warmth has hard limits here. One noteworthy example is the plight of LGBTQ+ people here, who cross them automatically.
nodes.ending: Of course, the old communal ways here are changing. Young people move to the city, get a job, get a phone, eat imported food, become part of the wider world, etc. (some of the men even make the dangerous journey by sea to Europe). So what about the families? The ones that used to share almost everything are now more reliant on cash and individual opportunities.

nodes.title: What Helps Communities Last—and Whether Longevity Is Enough
nodes.opening: Communities That Abide by Dmitry Orlov makes an uncomfortable argument: the communities that last a long time often rely on 1) communal property, 2) separation, 3) boundaries and 4) a binding ideology. From a distance, cohesion and capture can look a lot alike. Is longevity alone a meaningful measure, when a community may keep going without its members flourishing? That’s the question in “Measuring Success in Intentional Communities” , a paper by Rubin, Willis and Ludwig. Commitment and Community by Rosabeth Moss Kanter is a classic. It compares a bunch of nineteenth-century communes, and the practices that built commitment in them. Alienation and Charisma by Benjamin Zablocki is field research on communes, and on the role charisma plays in them. Jo Freeman’s “The Tyranny of Structurelessness” (1970) is the classic essay on hidden hierarchy. Can it be harder to challenge than explicit authority? She argues it can.

old_nodes.title: Why Communities Keep Dying in the Same Two Ways
old_nodes.opening: Most communes of my acquaintance traded inner freedom of the heart (spirituality) for outer freedom (secular, nondogmatic, political). The two pendulum ends of this trade-off mirror each other. I believe we can combine the best of both, but first, let’s see how each fails individually.
old_nodes.ending: To give an example of striking the balance: My contemplative practice is grounded in the early Buddhist suttas , with a critical reading. Most are treasure, while some are obviously late additions (sometimes to the point of real absurdity). A living community should relate to its own teachings in that same critical manner while staying devoted to following what they’ve decided on so far.

old_nodes.title: Outer-freedom-only models
old_nodes.opening: The secular communes (and all the manuals I’ve seen on building them) had a solution for how to distribute property or labor in a way folks could agree on, but when the deep waters of jealousy or childhood hurt or humiliation or attraction or resentment or grief came up, the group was without a common method for dealing with it.
old_nodes.ending: Eventually, when people are together long enough, politics will become a way of carrying emotional material that people can’t name. There will be a fight about a schedule or committee or noise or food or some policy or other, but it won’t be about that. There’s no shared way to talk about the hurt itself, but the meeting agenda is the one place the group lets you push for something and win, so the angry communard goes there, trying to get some justice.

old_nodes.title: Spiritual dogma models attempting inner freedom
old_nodes.opening: Many people already realized that are more interested in spiritual (or emotional) liberation than political liberation, so they tend to congregate in communities built for that. But because these communes focus so much on the inner work that the founder believes in, it can often look like some kind of prison-monestary cult, where you feel free inside as long as you don’t question anything.
old_nodes.ending: The Farm , in Tennessee, at its largest about 1,500 people, had many beautiful values. But in the early days, the community’s spirituality and social life followed the founder, Stephen Gaskin. From what former members have shared, the community’s doctrine ran deep into members’ intimate decisions. This is how it often goes: folks talk about oneness with the universe, while one man defines what the universe is.

old_nodes.title: We Want Freedom Inside & Out!
old_nodes.opening: Let’s face it: food, housing, and logistics are not enough reason to bind whole lives together. That’s more like a situationship . A community needs a shared sacred inner practice that gives the difficulty of our life together a deeper meaning. We help each other heal and choose love over fear. And we turn outward with a purpose, using the escuelita model to bring our healing to the world.
old_nodes.ending: To give an example of striking the balance: My contemplative practice is grounded in the early Buddhist suttas , with a critical reading. Most are treasure, while some are obviously late additions (sometimes to the point of real absurdity). A living community should relate to its own teachings in that same critical manner while staying devoted to following what they’ve decided on so far.

old_nodes.title: The Four Parts That Have to Pl/ork Together
old_nodes.opening: Communities tend to focus on the aspect of their project that was most interesting to the original founders, for example political types getting super into writing by-laws, or spiritual types just meditating all the time, or therapists processing each other, or people who like psychedelics discovering they’re all God together and never getting to the point of deciding who will put their name on the deed.
old_nodes.ending: The first three parts are the inside of the container, and this container is what gives those a stable place to manifest. It’s the practical logistical foundation that gets built once the architects can work well together.

old_nodes.title: 1. Inner pl/ork
old_nodes.opening: Probably the most obvious type of pl/ork is reparenting . Here’s an example: you teach your inner child geography, while s/he teaches you the world is a cat!
old_nodes.ending: And this reparenting journey is built on somatic regulation first. I.e., listening to the body’s feelings before making a decision with the mind. And that actually symbolizes the adult/child relationship to me in some way as well.

old_nodes.title: 2. Relational pl/ork
old_nodes.opening: Hearthwork distributes counseling among peers: equal time, attention without interpretation or fixing, and then you switch.
old_nodes.ending: Another thing is knowing which problems are beyond what peers can handle and need outside or expert help.

old_nodes.title: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
old_nodes.opening: In 2005, a few college buddies (Emile & Dolores) and I went down to Oventik, one of the Zapatista caracoles (”snails”), the regional centers that tie their villages together in Chiapas. We almost died several times getting there. The muddy mountain road ran along cliffs without guardrails, and our rental car was on its last legs, which is a great combination when you’re on your way to visit a revolution.

old_nodes.title: Democratic anarcho-communalism actualized
old_nodes.opening: What impressed me the most was how they do authority. It’s mandar obedeciendo , to lead by obeying: the representatives carry the decisions people made in the assemblies, and they have to answer to the people who gave them the mandate.
old_nodes.ending: The Fire and the Word describes the movement growing from family to village, village to region, and region to larger structures. It also gives one of the most useful Zapatista principles for community design: build the practice first and develop the theory afterward. The autonomous municipalities came first; an association of them became a rehearsal for the Good Government Juntas (Boards). When different municipalities encountered different problems and uneven progress, that experience generated another structure rather than being forced to fit the original plan.

old_nodes.title: Real democracy is a continual struggle
old_nodes.opening: After a long internal review, in 2023, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving their previous federated governmental structure, which was split into Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. The original idea was to have power vested in the local communities, but it had crept up and consolidated itself at higher levels over time for practical reasons. Their new arrangement moved authority downward toward a Local Autonomous Government in each community.
old_nodes.ending: But there is a special reason the Zapatistas were successfully able to reverse this degeneration. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories. They share language and family ties. They’ve fought land struggles together, and defended themselves together for decades.

old_nodes.title: Exporting Zapatismo via the Escuelita
old_nodes.opening: For the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita (little school). The goal of the escuelita was to expand their anarcho-communal, spiritual-humanist revolution worldwide. Outsiders came from all over the world, lived with host families there and learned autonomy by taking part in day to day life. Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.
old_nodes.ending: But despite actually trying to train people in their model, the Zapatistas themselves have been clear that people shouldn’t expect to directly or easily import/export their philosophy ( Zapatismo ) as something ready-made, shake & bake. A new ecovillage can’t copy the diagram everyone can see and get the trust underneath it right away.

old_nodes.title: Money is still a problem
old_nodes.opening: Now, the Zapatistas also don’t prove my whole money-free economy goal. They still use money internally in some cases, not others, and they still use it externally for trade. They’ve also benefitted from outside economic help, while at the same time making efforts to remain politically independent from donors and more self-sustaining.
old_nodes.ending: One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents spend their lives performing community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities there are. A week of feeling transformed isn’t what it’s for. It’s for teaching enough of the social and material system that some people can build somewhere else.

old_nodes.title: Are Zapatistas just unicorns?
old_nodes.opening: As part of my research I have also looked for evidence of what happened after the Escuelita . While I found information on alumni networks, people bringing practices back with them, and organizing later, I couldn’t find a clear chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita , then a new communal institution being set up, and then evidence about how its members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading abroad before the Escuelita , so if some institution resembles a Zapatista one later, that alone doesn’t prove the Escuelita was responsible.

old_nodes.title: Practicing Community Can Start Now
old_nodes.opening: I realize that for most people reading this there are a lot of reasons why they can’t just head off and go join or build community on some land. Jobs, kids, pets, debt, a mortgage, a sick parent, or several of these arranged in a circle... That’s fine! The most important pl/ork doesn’t need land anyway.
old_nodes.ending: None of this does away with scarcity or economic power. There are lots of areas where such power can be wielded: access to food storage, housing, tools, land, medicine, transportation, and the outside world’s currency, to name a few. Even in a moneyless community, someone can control what’s scarce. Who decides how these things are budgeted and distributed? What do members owe one another? old_nodes.title: Practice group of whom?
old_nodes.opening: Uh, but wait, where do you find these people? Try an unprogrammed Quaker or Unitarian meeting, a restorative-practice group, any open-hearted congregation, a mature recovery group, a meditation group, or find some people who have gone on long retreats and come back kinder, rather than more impressed with themselves.

old_nodes.ending: Are you willing to experiment? That’s a real value too. Put it on your list, because the people you live next to might think the experiment ended in 1978, and everything that came out of it is doctrine now.

I think the path there has three stages.

old_nodes.ending: They should not be demonized for not trying to fit in. They should be offered compassion, but ultimately it’s up to them if they want to fit in and follow the communal processes. And in some cases, the community may make exceptions. If someone is actually sick and needs care, kicking them out could be like a death sentence. So it’s up to the people involved.

old_nodes.title: Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution
old_nodes.opening: Good people leave for good reasons -- dying parent, love, work, health, exhaustion, change of mind, etc. You don’t want them to lose everything they’ve put in. That’s coercive -- they HAVE to stay if they can’t afford to go, and a community of prisoners isn’t ideal. Whether or not you use money, you’ll need to have a way of providing people with resources when they leave (cash, if you use it, but also tools, transportation, temporary housing, stored up goods, the right to keep using something, or whatever). Otherwise their “right” to leave is only on paper -- it only works when the community happens to have spare money. Write up the exit terms while leaving is still only theoretical -- like a pre-nup when you’re planning the wedding. Not romantic, but protective. Much easier than doing it once anybody’s furious.

The Farm’s communal economy had changed dramatically, but the bonds hadn’t vanished.

old_nodes.title: When Somebody Has to Go
old_nodes.opening: A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. There may be times when someone has to go. If someone is a serious or generalized danger to others, or keeps violating essential boundaries, or for whatever reason just makes everyday life together impossible for everyone else, it can be the right call to eject them. If restorative work can help in a reasonable amount of time, all the better. But it’s not the community’s job to be a treatment program for someone who’s endangering everyone else.
old_nodes.ending: Also decide on a mediator or ombudsperson in advance. Why bother? People often won’t trust someone they haven’t already met, who comes in during a crisis as a “neutral stranger.” A mediator doesn’t obviate the need for evidence, safeguarding, rulings, etc. Mediation is an attempt to restore good relations between people. When people can’t or won’t consent to being in community any more, they still need a final separation.

old_nodes.opening: Loneliness is only one reason building community feels urgent. I wrote separately about the wider polycrisis:
old_nodes.ending: On the other hand, while medical care is a big tripping point for communes, having social connections is measurably good for a person’s health. The Surgeon General’s advisory notes an increased risk for a range of health outcomes among people who are socially isolated. Community’s not a panacea, but it can make a difference, day to day, in the conditions people get sick, heal, age, and die in.

old_nodes.title: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
old_nodes.opening: Any community that lasts will eventually be reorganized by attraction and pair-bonding. When two exes live in the same city, they can move to different sides of the city. When they’re part of a thirty-person commune, they may still be in the same barn the next morning, working in the same team, attending the same meetings, sharing childcare and the same friends. A couple’s jealousy or breakup becomes a problem for the entire community, because it will change the loyalties, the sleeping arrangements, the labor, the kids, the alliances, and sometimes who’s leaving.
old_nodes.ending: There are some ways the group can help, and basic boundaries the group can enforce, without deciding what type of relationships people have. Even so, there will still be disagreements about this. That’s more realistic than saying it’s all been resolved.

old_nodes.title: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
old_nodes.opening: Couples who live together, share the same culture and even the same bed, still disagree about screens, vaccines, beans (vs meat), schooling , religion, discipline and medical care. And that’s just two people. Now think of twenty adults, all with different childhoods.
old_nodes.ending: Belonging and freedom should go hand in hand.

old_nodes.title: Communal Parenting Adds On
old_nodes.opening: One of the biggest reasons I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff’s The Continuum Concept . It’s one outsider’s interpretation of the Ye’kuana, an Indigenous people of the Venezuelan rainforest she lived with, and she may have idealized what she saw, but it’s still a powerful picture: the babies are carried along in ordinary adult life, the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and it doesn’t fall on one exhausted parent to be a child’s whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.
old_nodes.ending: Tamera’s Children’s Place has semi-repeated some of this old Kibbutz philosophy, taking children away from biological parents, because their founders’ ideology said that children are traumatized by the nuclear family and its unstable romantic underpinnings. On the other hand, their actual practice did allow parents (including fathers) to sometimes stay with their children in Children’s Place, so they weren’t as dogmatic as I originally thought.

old_nodes.title: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
old_nodes.opening: My own bias is still toward a system where kids are not solely taken care of by their parents, while still honoring the parent-child bond. If the father is unknown, the whole community can do the fathering, but the biological mom’s role should always be honored, since that attachment is formed already from years of nursing. Kids do need their own territory, places where they can create their own society, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.
old_nodes.ending: Sometimes we also need to protect people from the rare, but real threat posed by dangerous children. I looked through the research corpus for a well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to others. I was looking to find the reported conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I couldn’t find one. It’s possible that records are private, or that cases were referred elsewhere. Whatever the reason, I can’t claim communities already know how to handle the hardest cases on their own. In those cases, the child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review, hopefully including non-intrusive help from outside the home community.

So let them study, travel and make friends, encounter other ways of living, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors. And kids coming back isn’t necessarily the best thing for the communal movement either. If they then start their own communities, we may see more evolution than if they simply return and continue what their parents started.
old_nodes.ending: Belonging and freedom should go hand in hand.

old_nodes.title: Every childhood narrows the future
old_nodes.opening: Most ordinary parents aren’t going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, “Go see the world!” They’ll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work, so they can become self-sufficient, and eventually take care of their aging parents. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and basic survival may rightly come first.

old_nodes.title: 3: The Medicine Part - Yes, I’m Naming It
old_nodes.opening: Most of the writing on communities hasn’t caught up with psychedelics. They’ve gone from taboo toward regulated use really fast ( licensed service centers for psilocybin started opening in Oregon in 2023, Colorado set up a system for regulating natural medicines and began licensing in 2025, and New Mexico enacted a Medical Psilocybin Act in 2025), and Australia has allowed authorized psychiatrists limited access for a list of conditions since 2023, for both psilocybin and MDMA.
old_nodes.ending: Once the euphoria wears off and people have a more sober view of the call they feel, it can become useful. A community can be a place for people to train up in the practices, and sometimes go off and start another experiment. In fact, if people are training there so they can help others build communities of their own, they’d be working towards forming a real alternative. That answers the reasonable objection that communes are just privileged escape pods, which gets double dipped with the objection that psychedelics are also privileged escape pods (or, alternatively, as some say, “a vacation for the poor”).

old_nodes.title: Integration Starts Well Before Ceremony
old_nodes.opening: Using medicine is secondary to all of the other pl/ork that comes first: reparenting , developing somatic capacity , and learning to do peer counseling . The medicine can deepen an existing practice, but it can’t be a pharmacological shortcut to what takes several months of honest relationship with other people.
old_nodes.ending: As a community, you need to write down what is and isn’t allowed, and which activities are private (to the individual, to a group in the community, or to the community vs the outside).

old_nodes.title: Community Is What Makes Psychedelics Pl/ork Best!
old_nodes.opening: Part of it is integration: an insight needs somewhere to land. What happens when you come back from an amazing experience which gave you insight and clarity about your life, into the same old environment where nobody knows what you’ve been through and you’re faced with the same old cues? It can be super helpful to have gone through the experience in a community, where the people who held you through it can also notice what happens to you over the following months. The deeper you go, the more alienated you can feel. After my original ayahuasca ego deaths at age 25, I had trouble finding anyone in the physical world who seemed to have experienced anything similar. I couldn’t even find them at Buddhist monasteries despite all the preaching about enlightenment. That helped give me a God complex, a Savior complex, or both, which then attracted exactly the right people to show me my limits. 😂 In a community of people who’ve sat through the same nights, you aren’t the only one who’s been there, and someone can catch the God complex early. Do you trust the people you’re relying on for support? Support from people you trust is different from paid support, which is often paying people you don’t know to look after you for a night. Sometimes they’re great, but sometimes the person with the feather has only known you for 4 hours and already has a cosmology to explain everything you say. In a community, your sober sitter may be someone who’s known you for years, and you feel the difference between being watched and being held. This is especially important when doing iboga or other long and medically risky experiences. For those you need to be properly screened beforehand and monitored continuously. Your peers can also reality check any downloads you may have had. Psychedelics can give you insight and they can give you convincing nonsense, all in the same bright shining light. A few friends who know your history may notice the difference between new understanding and… mom. One of the benefits of community is rhythm , and many traditional medicinal practices occur within ceremonies that have a communal schedule. The shared schedule of ceremonies, rather than each person doing ceremonies when they want, can serve to limit compulsive use and provide for integration time. There are the practical benefits: logistics are easier when it comes to things like having childcare arranged by the group that parents are comfortable leaving their kid(s) with, not needing to drive away from the ceremony, having someone bring water to someone or just sit quietly with them while they come back to normal consciousness, etc. And if you scream in release, the neighbors and landlord don’t call 911. And then there will be people to play with! Raves often let strangers fast-track intimacy (getting to a level of intimacy that usually comes after building trust), but imagine doing ecstatic music & dance in a community that already knows each other (and each other’s inconvenient habits). 💃🕺

old_nodes.title: The Case Against Psychedelics
old_nodes.opening: If this article is going to be honest, it has to talk about both the value and the risk. Physical and psychological negative effects of ayahuasca were common in the Global Ayahuasca Survey , although severe effects were far less common and context mattered. And these medicines can open things up faster than a person (or their group) can deal with. One of the best resources on this topic is the Challenging Psychedelic Experiences project .

Any community based mainly around the peak experience is going to find out sooner or later that the insight doesn’t do the practical work for it. Sometimes the dishes need doing and a scared kid needs comforting.

old_nodes.title: No Special Shamans
old_nodes.opening: Traditional lineages usually disagree with me on this, and many ayahuasca tribes and Bwiti iboga communities believe the medicine should stay under trained lineage authority. I respect what those traditions have preserved, and I’ve learned some “dos & don’t dos” from their sensible practices and less sensible practices. For example, although I do highly value loving kindness meditation , inner child reparenting , and nibbana meditation before ceremony, during, and at all times, I notice a lot of people want their ceremony to look and feel like some kind of abstract mix of indigenous rituals & props to make it feel more authentic and sacred than their everyday life. I understand the benefit of setting aside one time and place for sacred experiences (the book, “God is Red” comes to mind), although the shadow side to that is making the spiritual seem like another world apart from your regular life, which is sort of opposite to integration.
old_nodes.ending: Still, I want people to learn to guide themselves and care for each other, within the limits of their competence.

old_nodes.title: After the Psychedelic Calling
old_nodes.opening: A lot of people feel the urge to form a village after going through some serious psychedelic and/or mystical experiences. Finding their people and helping others get to whatever just opened up is part of the same urge. That call may be real, but forming a community based on omnipotence is a terrible idea.
old_nodes.ending: Once the euphoria wears off and people have a more sober view of the call they feel, it can become useful. A community can be a place for people to train up in the practices, and sometimes go off and start another experiment. In fact, if people are training there so they can help others build communities of their own, they’d be working towards forming a real alternative. old_nodes.title: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
old_nodes.opening: I live in Sénégal, where “intentional community” often sounds like a strange Western phrase. People here are like, “Don’t human beings already do that?”
old_nodes.ending: But these days it can be soul destroying. People have a lot less of the communal life that held the obligation up (the shared land, work, childcare, food and daily belonging), but they still carry it. So if one of them makes it into the cash economy, it’s really hard to build any independence or long-term stability, because they may be expected to carry everybody. How can they get ahead, when all these people are dependent on them? And the relatives stay dependent too, since the payments don’t give them a real alternative. It’s the ancestral ethic playing out inside an individualistic cash economy. It can keep people alive, but it eats away at both sides too.

old_nodes.title: All is not well in paradise
old_nodes.opening: Does this mean I think Sénégal is some magical place that’s kept its communal paradise? No, not quite. The warmth has hard limits here. One noteworthy example is the plight of LGBTQ+ people here, who cross them automatically.
old_nodes.ending: Of course, the old communal ways here are changing. Young people move to the city, get a job, get a phone, eat imported food, become part of the wider world, etc. (some of the men even make the dangerous journey by sea to Europe). So what about the families? The ones that used to share almost everything are now more reliant on cash and individual opportunities.

old_nodes.title: Lessons from the Black Tax
old_nodes.opening: Then there’s the so-called “Black Tax,” a strange legacy of the old communal system: if you’ve got any money at all, you’re expected to share it with your parents, your siblings, your cousins, to pay school fees, medical bills, funerals, etc. I understand the instinct. In the ancestral way of doing things nobody made it alone, and the people who fed and raised you had a real claim on whatever prosperity came through you later. So why not share in return? That’s how the whole organism survived (it wasn’t charity).
old_nodes.ending: But these days it can be soul destroying. old_nodes.title: A Hope For Humanity
old_nodes.opening: Decades after the Bruderhof shaped my father, I’m publishing the film he made, and writing this.
old_nodes.ending: I am not currently recruiting anyone or founding a community, which makes it easier for me to write an article like this, since I’m not trying to get you onto my land. I do plan to find some land, and people may naturally end up living around me. All of the warnings in this article apply to me, too. old_nodes.title: What Helps Communities Last—and Whether Longevity Is Enough
old_nodes.opening: Communities That Abide by Dmitry Orlov makes an uncomfortable argument: the communities that last a long time often rely on 1) communal property, 2) separation, 3) boundaries and 4) a binding ideology. From a distance, cohesion and capture can look a lot alike. Is longevity alone a meaningful measure, when a community may keep going without its members flourishing? That’s the question in “Measuring Success in Intentional Communities” , a paper by Rubin, Willis and Ludwig. Commitment and Community by Rosabeth Moss Kanter is a classic. It compares a bunch of nineteenth-century communes, and the practices that built commitment in them. Alienation and Charisma by Benjamin Zablocki is field research on communes, and on the role charisma plays in them. Jo Freeman’s “The Tyranny of Structurelessness” (1970) is the classic essay on hidden hierarchy. Can it be harder to challenge than explicit authority? She argues it can.

excerpts.text: Most of the writing on communities hasn’t caught up with psychedelics. They’ve gone from taboo toward regulated use really fast ( licensed service centers for psilocybin started opening in Oregon in 2023, Colorado set up a system for regulating natural medicines and began licensing in 2025, and New Mexico enacted a Medical Psilocybin Act in 2025), and Australia has allowed authorized psychiatrists limited access for a list of conditions since 2023, for both psilocybin and MDMA.

That said, it’s not a smooth ride or an inevitability. The US FDA issued a Complete Response Letter to the MDMA-assisted therapy application in 2024, where they did not approve it and requested more evidence. And the thing with Portugal is that many people will lazily say “they’ve legalized everything there” - but that’s false, they’ve only decriminalized possessing small quantities for personal use . It’s still a crime to traffic drugs.

All of which means the legality of psychedelics varies by country and by state. It varies by substance, too. And it depends on a group’s religious status and on what exactly it does. So if psychedelic medicine is going to be part of a community at all, that community should definitely get actual local legal advice.

Most intentional communities using psychedelics are still not public about it, due to possible trouble (even where the law allows some use) from parents worried about children, from neighbors imagining chaos, from insurance providers who might drop them, and from local officials who may not understand any of the distinctions.

excerpts.text: If the community dissolves, what happens to the land and any outside debts? What about its buildings, equipment, common stores or funds? What happens to each member’s agreed rights? More immediately, who is responsible for ensuring that everyone has a place to live and food to eat? Who takes responsibility for making sure people get their medications and the other care they need? Who keeps childcare going, and makes sure the kids’ schooling carries on? Who takes responsibility for transportation, for the records, for family contact, for the animals, for making sure land obligations are met, and for any unresolved claims? That’s a lot of loose ends!

Think of it like a living will, and assign a bridge or successor for each critical function in advance, so basic life doesn’t depend on reviving the commune. The institution may not be salvageable, but who’s making breakfast tomorrow?
